title: What Each File Wants
dek: There is no best compressor, only a best match between what a file is and how it will be read. A measured field guide, October 2026: JSON at rest and on the wire, small messages and dictionaries, binary encodings, config files, logs, tables, images, audio and video — which codec, which level or quality, when a format beats a compressor, and when to leave a file alone.
byline: 9 October 2026 · Every recommendation backed by a measurement on this machine with recorded tool versions, or by a cited source; the XO examples are read from its tree
description: A measured field guide to compressing JSON, config files, logs, tabular data, images, audio and video in 2026: codecs, levels, dictionaries, columnar encodings and media codecs, and when not to compress.
og_description: zstd vs brotli vs gzip on JSON, dictionaries for small messages, CBOR and MessagePack vs compressed JSON, config files that grow, logs by block size, Parquet vs gzip'd CSV, AVIF and JPEG XL, Opus and FLAC, x264 vs x265 vs SVT-AV1 by VMAF — all measured, October 2026.
twitter_description: No best compressor, only the right match. JSON, config, logs, tables, images, audio and video — measured, with the codec and level each one wants.
badges_callout:
How to read the badges

from the spec marks text from an RFC or a format specification. from the docs marks a project's own documentation, release notes, wiki or a maintainer's words, including benchmarks others published, which are reported as their claims. from the tree marks something read from the XO source trees on this machine. measured here marks a result produced by _compute.py beside this page, with the exact tool versions recorded in _numbers.json, on one shared 2-CPU Linux machine: sizes, ratios and quality scores are exact for these inputs; speeds are tiers. reconstruction marks a judgement or recipe I have worked out rather than read.

sections.title: Every file wants something different
sections.brief: Thesis: there is no best compressor, only a best match between what a file is and how it will be read. Three questions decide: is the data already entropy-coded (images, audio, video, archives — then a general-purpose codec does nothing and the work is choosing the media codec and its quality); is it small (under a few hundred bytes framing dominates and compression grows it); and how will it be read (once over HTTP, many times from disk, randomly by offset, by column). 'The answer, up front' (h3, reconstruction, every row backed by a measured result later): JSON over HTTP → brotli or zstd at the CDN, gzip as fallback; JSON at rest → zstd level 3–9, with a trained dictionary for many small documents and batching for streams; config files (TOML, YAML, small JSON) → do not compress individually; lockfiles and bundles → whatever the registry uses (gzip -9 tarballs); JSONL logs → zstd in large blocks, seekable if you need random access; tabular data → Parquet with dictionary/RLE encodings and zstd, not gzip'd CSV; images → AVIF or JPEG XL for photos, lossless WebP or oxipng'd PNG for graphics; audio → Opus for listening, FLAC for archive; video → AV1 via SVT-AV1 at a CRF for storage and modern clients, H.264 for universal playback, HEVC where hardware demands it; anything already compressed → store it, never gzip it. Point to the theory companion ../what-compression-keeps/ and to the TOML/JSON/YAML guide ../what-the-parser-hears/.

fig-headline · the measured headline per data type (stat tiles, measured) · one tile per type: the best measured ratio or size reduction and the codec that achieved it, from _numbers.json.

sections.title: How the measurements were made
sections.brief: Method, so every later number can be judged. Machine: Ubuntu 26.04.1, 2 vCPU in a shared cgroup, 31 GiB RAM (inventory.md section 1); tool versions exactly as recorded in _numbers.json → versions (Python 3.14.4 compression.zstd on libzstd 1.5.7, brotli, gzip/zlib, xz, lz4, pyarrow, Pillow, libjxl, oxipng, FFmpeg static build with x264/x265/SVT-AV1/libvmaf, FLAC, Opus — whatever the harness actually used). Corpora: list each with its size, source and licence (from _numbers.json → corpora): JSON (this site's posts.json, what-the-parser-hears/_numbers.json, synthetic API records), small JSON documents (for dictionaries), TOML/YAML config files and Cargo.lock files from the trees, JSONL logs (a real XO audit log, ratios only), a tabular dataset, images, an audio clip and a video clip (Blender Foundation's Tears of Steel is CC BY 3.0 for the film; its soundtrack files are CC BY-ND — inventory.md myth; use media licence-clean for measurement and say exactly which file). What is exact (bytes, ratios, quality scores) and what is not (speeds on a contended 2-CPU machine: tiers only, with the repeat count and median). Private corpora (Claude session logs, ~/.quirq logs) are used for aggregate ratios only, never quoted — say so if used at all. How to rerun: uv run _compute.py; FFmpeg static build location.
figures: fig-corpora · the test corpora (HTML table) · name, type, bytes, files, source, licence, what it stands for.

sections.title: JSON: pick a level, then stop
sections.brief: Measured on the JSON corpora (_numbers.json → json): ratio and compression/decompression speed tiers for gzip -1/-6/-9, zlib-ng or libdeflate if used, brotli 1/5/9/11, zstd 1/3/9/19 (and --ultra -22), xz -6/-9, lz4; the knee of the curve (where extra level buys little); brotli's default quality 11 vs zstd's 3 (codecs.md: default-vs-default misleads). Minified vs pretty: raw sizes and compressed sizes — compression erases most of the difference (structured.md section 1; Python json.dumps default separators are not minimal). Published claims to set beside ours, as claims: Viotti & Kinderkhedia 2022 on SchemaStore JSON; Facebook's 2016 zstd dictionary result; the 'Brotli 20–26% better than gzip' misattribution (it was against Zopfli). HTTP specifics belong to ../what-compression-keeps/#on-the-wire — link, do not repeat. Recommend: zstd 3 at rest by default, 9–19 for cold archives; brotli 5–6 dynamic and 11 for static at the edge; gzip -6 when only gzip exists.
figures: fig-json-frontier · JSON: ratio vs speed (SVG chart, wide, measured) · one point per codec/level on the main JSON corpus; compression speed on x (log), ratio on y; decompression speed as a second marker; the knee annotated.
fig-minify · pretty vs minified, before and after compression (SVG bars, measured) · raw, gzip -6, brotli 11, zstd 3 for pretty and minified versions of the same documents.

sections.title: Small messages and dictionaries
sections.brief: Compression needs repetition, and a 300-byte message has little. Framing: gzip ≥ 18 bytes, zstd ≥ 9 (structured.md F127, F129); GNU gzip compresses 'even if the compressed file is slightly larger'; Viotti: LZMA reached −171.4% on one tiny document; GZIP best from 100 bytes up. Measured (_numbers.json → small): per-document compression of many small JSON documents (sizes 100 B–4 KB) with gzip, brotli, zstd; then zstd with a trained dictionary (dictionary sizes 4/16/64/110 KB; train/test split stated; Python compression.zstd.train_dict), then batching N documents per frame (Kafka's design doc: redundancy lies between messages, so batches compress — structured.md F17). Show where the dictionary beats batching (random access to single messages) and its operational cost (dictionary distribution and versioning; RFC 9842 makes this a web standard — link to the deep-dive). Facebook 2016: 1,000 GitHub user records ~850 KB → ~300 KB per-file → 122 KB with a 64 KB dictionary (as their claim).
figures: fig-small · small messages: per-message vs dictionary vs batch (SVG, wide, measured) · ratio by message size bucket for no compression, gzip, zstd, zstd+dictionary, zstd batched; the break-even line at 1.0×.
fig-dict-size · how big a dictionary (SVG, measured) · ratio vs dictionary size for the small-document corpus.

sections.title: Binary encodings vs compressed text
sections.brief: Does switching format beat compressing JSON? Measured (_numbers.json → binary): the same documents as JSON, minified JSON, CBOR (RFC 8949), MessagePack, BSON, and — if the harness can define a schema cheaply — Protobuf or Avro; each raw and with zstd 3 and gzip -6. Sourced context: Viotti & Kinderkhedia — against compressed JSON, schema-less binary formats give negative median and average reductions whether or not they are compressed; compressed schema-driven formats (ASN.1 PER, Avro, Protobuf) beat compressed JSON in every case tested; BSON is sometimes larger than JSON per its own FAQ; UBJSON concedes gzip's ~75% vs its ~30%; Protobuf docs: 'Messages are not compressed.' Conclusion: binary formats buy parse speed and types, not size; size comes from schemas or compression.
figures: fig-binary · one record set in six encodings, raw and compressed (SVG grouped bars, measured).

sections.title: Config files: leave them alone
sections.brief: TOML, YAML and small JSON config files are usually under a few KB: measured (_numbers.json → config) — every TOML/YAML/JSON config file found in the XO trees compressed individually with gzip/brotli/zstd: how many grew, median ratio, and the size where compression starts to pay. Cargo.lock as the large TOML case (up to 134 KB in the trees): ratio per codec. What registries already do: crates.io .crate = tar.gz built with Compression::best(); npm/pacote level 9 with a fixed 1985 mtime for reproducibility; wheels are ZIP, sdists .tar.gz; Git zlib-compresses loose objects (level 1 default) and delta-compresses packs (structured.md section 13). xo-space's sync tarball uses gzip level 6 but its header carries the current time, so the bytes change every run (inventory.md section 16, cite path:line) — the reproducibility fix is mtime=0 (reconstruction, show the 1-line change).
figures: fig-config · config files individually compressed (SVG scatter or bars, measured) · original size vs compressed/original for each file; the 1.0 line; Cargo.lock points labelled.

sections.title: Logs and JSON Lines
sections.brief: Streams of similar records compress extremely well if the compressor sees enough of them at once. Measured (_numbers.json → logs) on a real JSONL audit log from the XO trees (doomfly audit.jsonl, 6.1 MB — ratios only) and a synthetic access log: ratio vs block size (1 KB … 4 MB) for gzip, zstd 3, zstd 19, xz; DuckDB's table (zstd ×1.72 at 1 kB, ×2.73 at 1 MB; blocks ≥ 256 kB) as a published comparison; random access: the zstd seekable format (contrib) — measured overhead of seek tables at frame sizes 64 KB/1 MB. Tree data point: doomfly's hourly gzip -9 archive 6,123,015 → 717,390 B, 8.54× (inventory.md). Specialised log compressors as claims: CLP (OSDI 2021) about 2× gzip's ratio; Uber 169× on Spark logs; µSlope (OSDI 2024) 21.9:1–186.8:1 on JSON logs, 2.34× zstd; Loki defaults to gzip chunks; Elasticsearch best_compression is ZSTD since 8.16. Agent transcripts: Claude Code keeps plaintext JSONL for 30 days; Gemini CLI appends uncompressed JSONL; Codex has a default-off zstd cold-rollout compressor and zstd-compresses API request bodies by default (structured.md section 15). Measured on private session logs only as an aggregate ratio, if the harness did so (no content).
figures: fig-blocks · ratio rises with block size (SVG line chart, wide, measured) · ratio vs block size for each codec on the JSONL corpus; the 256 kB mark.
fig-agent-logs · what agent tools do with their transcripts (stack rows) · Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI: format, retention, compression, source.

sections.title: Tables: let the format do the work
sections.brief: For tabular data, encoding beats compression. Measured (_numbers.json → tables) on one dataset (synthetic but realistic, or a public licence-clean CSV; say which): CSV raw, CSV.gz, CSV.zst, Parquet with no codec, snappy, zstd (levels), lz4_raw, gzip; with and without dictionary encoding; Arrow IPC with zstd; and DuckDB native if available. Parquet internals (structured.md section 7, quote the spec): PLAIN, RLE/bit-packing hybrid, dictionary, DELTA_BINARY_PACKED, DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY, BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT (does not shrink by itself), ALP (encoding 10, 'Preview', parquet-format 2.14.0 on 2026-09-11); legacy LZ4 deprecated for LZ4_RAW; default codecs differ by writer (pyarrow/DuckDB/Spark snappy, Polars zstd); ORC defaults to ZSTD since 2.0.0; DuckDB lightweight compression (RLE, bitpacking, FSST, ALP since 0.10.0, zstd for long strings since 1.2.0); ClickHouse codecs (Delta, DoubleDelta, Gorilla, T64, ZSTD default level 1; ALP in 26.3, beta in 26.9); Gorilla (VLDB 2015), FSST (VLDB 2020), ALP (SIGMOD 2024). PostgreSQL TOAST: pglz default in 14–18, lz4 default in 19 when built with it (link ../where-the-json-lives/).
figures: fig-tables · one table, nine encodings (SVG bars, wide, measured) · bytes for CSV, CSV.gz, CSV.zst, Parquet none/snappy/zstd/lz4_raw/gzip, Arrow IPC zstd; with read-time tiers if measured.
fig-parquet · inside a Parquet column chunk (SVG) · values → dictionary page + RLE/bit-packed indices → codec; where each encoding applies.

sections.title: Images
sections.brief: Images are already compressed; the choice is the codec and the quality. Measured (_numbers.json → images) on a small licence-clean set (photographic and graphic; say exactly which files and licences): PNG as-is vs oxipng (lossless), lossless WebP, lossless JPEG XL; for photos, JPEG (Pillow/libjpeg-turbo or mozjpeg/jpegli if available) vs WebP vs AVIF vs JPEG XL at matched quality — bytes at a fixed SSIMULACRA 2 or butteraugli/SSIM target if the harness has a metric (say which), plus encode time tiers; JPEG → JPEG XL lossless recompression (Apple/WebKit's 'average of 20%' claim vs measured). Browser support as of 9 Oct 2026 (media.md section 10): JPEG XL back in Chrome 155 stable (2026-10-06) via the Rust jxl-rs decoder, Firefox planned for 158 (2026-10-13), Safari partial since 17; AVIF and WebP universal per caniuse (verify in dossier). gzip on a JPEG/PNG: measured ~0 gain (MDN advises against HTTP-compressing images). SVG is text: gzip/brotli it (this site's 22 SVGs as a data point).
figures: fig-images · bytes at equal quality (SVG, wide, measured) · per image: JPEG, WebP, AVIF, JPEG XL bars at the matched quality target; lossless group: PNG, oxipng, WebP lossless, JXL lossless.
fig-image-support · where each image format decodes, October 2026 (HTML table) · Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge; with versions and dates from the dossier.

sections.title: Audio
sections.brief: Lossless: FLAC (RFC 9639, Dec 2024; FLAC 1.5.0 multithreaded encoding) vs ALAC vs WAV; measured FLAC levels 0/5/8 ratio on a licence-clean clip. Lossy: Opus (RFC 6716, RFC 8251; libopus 1.6 added 96 kHz 'Opus HD' and an ML bandwidth extension; 1.6.1 current) — Xiph's recommended bitrates (24/32 kb/s podcasts, 64–96 streaming, 96–128 storage; FLAC for archiving); AAC; MP3 (patents expired 2017). Measured (_numbers.json → audio): the clip as WAV, FLAC -5/-8, Opus 32/64/96/128 kb/s, and AAC or MP3 if the FFmpeg build has an encoder — bytes and, if available, a quality metric (ViSQOL is unlikely; if none, say so and give bytes only). gzip/zstd on FLAC or Opus: ~0 gain.
figures: fig-audio · one minute of audio, eight ways (SVG bars, measured) · bytes per encoding with bitrate labels; the lossless group separated.

sections.title: Video
sections.brief: Video is where codec choice moves the most bytes. Status as of 9 Oct 2026 (media.md sections 0–8): H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC, VP9, AV1, H.266/VVC, AV2 (spec v1.0.0 dated 28 May 2026, announced 9 June 2026, AOMedia's claim ~30% over AV1; no FFmpeg support, no caniuse entry, no hardware). Licensing: Access Advance acquired Via LA's HEVC/VVC programme on 15 Dec 2025 ('VCL Advance'); Access Advance's VDP pool covers streaming for HEVC, VVC, VP9 and AV1; Sisvel's AV1 pool EUR 0.32/0.24 per display device; Via LA H.264 streaming fees up to $4.5M a year. Support: Safari AV1 hardware-only; Chrome HEVC platform-dependent. Encoders: x264, x265, SVT-AV1 4.2.0 (4.0.0 raised CRF to 1–70 in 0.25 steps; defaults preset 8, CRF 35; FFmpeg's libsvtav1 still caps -crf at 63 — libsvtav1.c:826), libaom, rav1e, VVenC; FFmpeg 9.0.2 is current (the FFmpeg wiki guides are partly stale). Measured (_numbers.json → video) on one licence-clean 1080p clip (state source, duration, frames, licence): x264 CRF 18/23/28 (preset medium), x265 CRF 23/28/32, SVT-AV1 CRF 25/35/45 at preset 8 (and 10 for speed), VP9 if time allows — bytes, bitrate, VMAF (libvmaf model as recorded; Netflix's VMAF v1 models exist but FFmpeg's filter defaults to vmaf_v0.6.1 — say which was used), encode time tiers; derive BD-rate of x265 and SVT-AV1 vs x264 over the VMAF range covered (method draft-ietf-netvc-testing-09 §4.2) — only if at least 3 points per codec overlap. Also: remux (container change) costs nothing and changes no bytes of video; gzip/zstd on the MP4 saves ~0 (measured); 10-bit for 8-bit sources costs ~5% more bytes for slightly better fidelity per SVT-AV1 docs. Industry: Netflix AV1 'over a third' of global VOD (Sept 2026); Netflix film-grain synthesis cut bitrate 36% at 1080p+ (July 2025); Meta AV1 >70% of watch time; Netflix 2018: real generational gains closer to 40% than the claimed 50%. Recipes (reconstruction, each backed by the measurement): archive → SVT-AV1 preset 4–6 CRF ~30; web → AV1 with H.264 fallback; editing proxies → H.264 high bitrate or intra.

sections.title: Already compressed: leave it
sections.brief: Measured (_numbers.json → recompress): gzip -9, zstd 19, xz -9 and brotli 11 on a JPEG, a PNG, an MP4, an Opus/FLAC file, a .zip and a .tar.gz — gains (or growth) to the byte; then zstd on a tar of mixed already-compressed media. Why: CABAC and AV1's adaptive-CDF arithmetic coding, DEFLATE inside PNG, etc. (media.md section 1). Exceptions with real gains: PNG → oxipng/zopfli (re-does the DEFLATE), JPEG → JPEG XL lossless recompression, ZIP → re-pack with a stronger codec, double-compressed data (Arrow's spec: 'double compression typically worsens performance'). HTTP: MDN advises against Content-Encoding for images/audio/video; nginx gzips only text/html by default; Cloudflare/Vercel compress only an allowlist of MIME types.
figures: fig-recompress · compressing the already compressed (SVG bars, measured) · saving (%) per file type per codec, mostly within ±1%; the exceptions (oxipng, JXL recompression) shown separately.

sections.title: A practice that holds
sections.brief: Rules, each tied to a measured or sourced result above: (1) decide by data type and read pattern, not by codec fame; (2) zstd 3 is the default for data at rest; brotli/zstd at the edge for text; (3) never compress tiny payloads individually — batch or use a dictionary, and version the dictionary; (4) for tables, use a columnar format before a codec; (5) for media, choose codec and quality, measure with a perceptual metric, keep the source; (6) do not compress already-compressed data; (7) record codec, level and dictionary id with the data (zstd frame headers carry a dictionary ID; Parquet records codec per column chunk); (8) bound decompression (max output size, ratio limits) — decompression bombs and the YAML alias bomb are one family; (9) never compress secrets together with attacker-controlled input over the wire (BREACH) — link to ../what-compression-keeps/#hazards; (10) make archives reproducible (fixed mtime, sorted entries — npm's 1985 mtime, xo-space's gzip header). Then 'Where this breaks' (h3): one machine, contended CPU (speed tiers only); one clip/image set; quality metrics are models of perception, not perception; codec versions move fast — check the date. Close with the decision rule paragraph mirroring the answer up front.
figures: fig-checklist · per data type: codec, level/quality, container, how to verify (stack rows, wide).

sections.title: Sources
sections.brief: Grouped: Specifications (RFC 1950–1952, 7932, 8878, 9659, 9842, 8949 CBOR, 9639 FLAC, 6716/8251 Opus, Parquet format spec, AV1 spec, AV2 announcement); Codec and tool docs (zstd, brotli, zlib-ng, libdeflate, xz, lz4, oxipng, libjxl, libavif/Pillow, mozjpeg/jpegli, FFmpeg + wiki, SVT-AV1 docs, x264/x265, libvmaf, FLAC, Opus wiki, pyarrow, DuckDB, ClickHouse, Elasticsearch, Loki, Kafka design doc); Published measurements cited as claims (Viotti & Kinderkhedia 2022, Facebook zstd 2016, DuckDB, CLP OSDI 2021, µSlope OSDI 2024, Uber, Netflix tech blog posts, Meta AV1, Apple/WebKit JPEG XL); Browser and licensing status (caniuse, chromestatus, MDN, Access Advance, Sisvel, Via LA); Test media and licences; XO trees read. Measurement: _compute.py, _numbers.json, tool versions, how to rerun. Then the .footnote provenance: sourced facts dated 8–9 October 2026; measured results with exact tool versions on one shared 2-CPU machine (sizes/ratios/quality exact for these inputs, speeds tiers); reconstruction = the recipes and decision rules; not verified = anything the text relies on from the dossiers' open questions. Only URLs that appear in the dossiers.
